# Travel Support

`customer_support.model.b2c.travel` · vertical · parent `customer_support.model.b2c`

> Supporting travellers before, during and after a trip. Two structural facts do all the work here, and both are about time. The clock is a departure, and it is unforgiving. The same contact — "my booking is wrong" — is a routine amendment three weeks out and an emergency ninety minutes before a gate closes, because after the cutoff the cheap remedy stops existing and only the expensive, manual, supplier-dependent one remains. Time-to-departure, not severity and not arrival order, is the correct queue ordering, and a triage model that ignores it will handle contacts in the order that maximises the number of people who miss their trip. Disruption arrives as a cohort. Weather, strikes, cancellations and technical events do not produce a gradual rise; they produce every affected passenger contacting simultaneously, through every channel, about the same event, with the same three questions. Handling that as individual tickets guarantees that most people are answered after the situation has already resolved itself badly. Underneath both, the remedy usually belongs to somebody else. Fare rules, carrier policy, hotel terms and supplier refund latency bound what may be offered, and duty-of-care obligations to a stranded passenger apply regardless of whose fault it was. The error carried in from consumer ecommerce is treating this as a refunds queue. A refund is the worst available outcome for someone standing in an airport — what they need is to still travel — and an operator who reaches for money first has solved the wrong problem expensively.


## Characteristics

|  |  |
|---|---|
| requester | the traveller, often mid-journey, frequently on a phone, in another timezone, with a deadline they cannot move and sometimes without connectivity |
| typical_resolution_hours | 3 |
| volume_shape | seasonal baseline plus violent event-driven surges — one weather system or strike can produce a day's volume in an hour, entirely from one affected cohort |
| staffing_model | pooled agents with an in-trip/disruption desk held separate from pre-travel sales and post-travel claims |
| coverage | 24x7 and genuinely global; someone is always mid-journey somewhere |
| automation_level | high on pre-travel self-service and check-in, deliberately lower in-trip — a bot that cannot rebook is an obstacle to a passenger at a gate |
| notes | The three phases — pre-travel, in-trip, post-travel — behave like three different support organisations sharing a brand. Staffing and measuring them as one queue is the most common structural error in this vertical.  |

## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.ticket`

Requires `priority`, `resolution_target_at`


> The resolution target is the departure, not a service promise. When the contractual clock and the flight disagree the flight wins, and any system that only knows the contractual clock will report a healthy queue while the cabin doors close.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.incident`

Requires `affected_customer_count`, `blast_radius`, `broadcast_cadence_minutes`


> Blast radius here is a route, a date and a supplier, which makes the affected population exactly enumerable in advance of them contacting us. That is unusual and it is the whole opportunity: a disruption is one of the few consumer events where proactive contact can genuinely empty the queue that is about to form.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.requester`

Requires `timezone`, `preferred_channel`, `language`


> A traveller is by definition not where they normally are. Their local time, the channel that works on foreign data roaming, and the language they need under stress are all different from what their profile says, and getting any of the three wrong turns a recoverable situation into an unreachable one.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.customer_sentiment`

Requires `public_exposure`


> Distress in transit is qualitatively different from dissatisfaction with a purchase, and it photographs well. Reading it as ordinary consumer anger under-rates both the human situation and the reputational one.
